title: Enterprise RAG for Technical Knowledge
subtitle: How organizations can turn technical documents into secure, citation-backed AI knowledge systems

heroImage.alt: Engineer using an AI-enabled technical knowledge system beside manuals and engineering equipment
heroImage.caption: Technical expertise becomes easier to access when people and trusted knowledge work together.

humanImpactImage.alt: Engineering team collaborating around an AI-supported technical knowledge workflow
humanImpactImage.caption: The outcome is faster answers, better decisions, and shared technical knowledge.

summary.problem: Technical knowledge is often spread across manuals, procedures, drawings, service notes, tables, and controlled documents. People spend time searching, and answers can become unsafe when they are based on outdated or inaccessible material.
summary.solution: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) connects a language model to an organization's approved knowledge sources. Search retrieves relevant evidence first, then the model explains that evidence in a natural way with citations.
businessValue: Less repeated searching and onboarding effort
Traceable answers instead of unsupported guesses
Security rules applied before confidential content is retrieved
architecture: Documents -> parse and normalize -> split into chunks -> create embeddings -> index
Question -> authorize -> hybrid retrieve -> rerank -> build context -> answer with citations
Monitoring -> evaluate quality, cost, latency, access decisions, and failures
summary.cost: Ingestion is mostly an initial and update-driven cost. Query cost is a fixed platform baseline plus usage-based model, embedding, reranking, and transaction costs.

sections.title: The Business Problem
content: Important technical knowledge is rarely stored in one clean database. It is distributed across long documents, scanned pages, spreadsheets, diagrams, and versioned procedures. A person may know that an answer exists but still spend minutes or hours locating the right passage.
An enterprise assistant must do more than produce fluent text. It must use approved information, respect access rights, identify the source and version, and make uncertainty visible.

image.alt: Technical knowledge spread across manuals, spreadsheets, diagrams, and document versions
image.caption: Technical knowledge becomes difficult to use when it is distributed across disconnected sources.

callouts: The goal is not to replace expert judgment. The goal is to reduce time spent finding and interpreting trusted information.

sections.title: What is an LLM?
content: A large language model (LLM) is a model trained to recognize patterns in text and generate a likely continuation. It processes text as small units called tokens and uses learned statistical relationships to produce an answer.
An LLM can explain, summarize, translate, classify, and draft. It does not automatically know an organization's private documents, current procedures, or who is allowed to see them.
callouts: Simple explanation: an LLM is a powerful language engine, not a private document library.

sections.title: Why an LLM Alone is Not Enough
content: A model's training data may be old, incomplete, or unrelated to an organization's internal processes. Without retrieved evidence, it may confidently produce a plausible but unsupported answer. This behavior is commonly called hallucination.
Fine-tuning changes model behavior and style, but it is not a dependable replacement for a searchable, versioned knowledge source. Enterprise answers need current evidence and access-aware retrieval.

image.alt: Comparison between an LLM alone and a retrieval-augmented system using organization documents
image.caption: Retrieval gives the model current organizational evidence instead of asking it to answer from memory alone.

sections.title: What is RAG?
content: Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, is a pattern that searches trusted content before asking an LLM to answer. The retrieved passages are placed into the model's context, which is the information available for that request.
A good RAG system separates retrieval from generation. Search decides which evidence is relevant; the model turns that evidence into a useful explanation and cites the supporting sources.

image.alt: RAG workflow showing ask, retrieve, rerank, generate, and cite
image.caption: A simplified RAG query flow: ask, retrieve, rerank, generate, and cite.

callouts: RAG = retrieve evidence first, then generate an answer grounded in that evidence.

sections.title: High-Level Architecture
content: The system has two cooperating paths. The ingestion path prepares documents for search. The user-query path authenticates the person, retrieves permitted evidence, constructs a grounded prompt, and returns an answer with citations.

Typical Azure building blocks include Blob Storage for source files, Azure AI Document Intelligence for parsing and OCR, Azure OpenAI for generation and embeddings, Azure AI Search for retrieval, a relational database for control metadata, Microsoft Entra ID for identity, Key Vault for secrets, and Application Insights for telemetry.

image.alt: Enterprise RAG architecture showing ingestion and user query pipelines
image.caption: A bird's-eye view of the ingestion and user-query paths.

sections.title: Document Ingestion Pipeline
content: Ingestion is the controlled process of turning a source file into searchable records. A production pipeline records the source URI, checksum, document version, parser status, access labels, timestamps, and failure state before it publishes anything to the live index.
The pipeline should be asynchronous so large batches do not block users. Queues, retries, idempotency keys, and dead-letter handling make repeated or failed processing safe.

image.alt: Documents being parsed and transformed into structured searchable knowledge
image.caption: Raw documents become structured, searchable knowledge through controlled ingestion.

callouts: Idempotency means processing the same input twice does not create duplicate knowledge or corrupt the index.

sections.title: Document Parsing and OCR
content: Parsing extracts text, headings, page boundaries, tables, captions, and layout from digital documents. OCR, or optical character recognition, converts text inside scanned images into machine-readable text.

Azure AI Document Intelligence is one practical option for layout-aware extraction. The output should retain page numbers and element relationships so citations can point back to a human-readable location.

sections.title: Chunking
content: A chunk is a smaller logical section of a large document. Chunks make retrieval precise enough to fit useful evidence into the model context. Splitting only by character count can separate a heading from its explanation, so structure-aware splitting is usually better.

Chunk size, overlap, heading inheritance, table handling, and page boundaries should be tested against real questions. Overlap repeats a small boundary region so meaning is less likely to be lost between chunks.
callouts: A chunk should be understandable on its own while still carrying its document, section, page, and permission metadata.

sections.title: Tokens
content: A token is a small unit of text processed by an LLM. A word may be one token or several, and punctuation can also be tokenized. Token counts influence context limits, latency, and model cost.
Chunking by tokens rather than only characters gives more predictable prompt sizes. The correct limit depends on the embedding model, generation model, and the amount of evidence the answer needs.

sections.title: Metadata
content: Metadata is structured information attached to a document or chunk. Useful fields include document ID, title, section, page, source system, owner, publication date, effective date, version, language, equipment family, confidentiality label, and allowed groups.
Metadata supports filtering, citations, lifecycle management, analytics, and security. It should be validated like any other data because a wrong access label can expose the wrong evidence.

sections.title: Images, Tables and Graphs
content: Technical meaning is often carried by a wiring diagram, table, chart, or annotated image rather than ordinary paragraphs. The ingestion pipeline should preserve the original asset, extract nearby captions and labels, and create a searchable description when appropriate.

Tables may be normalized into structured rows as well as a readable text representation. Graphs should retain titles, axes, units, legends, and key observations. For safety-critical material, link the answer back to the original page or image instead of relying only on a generated description.

image.alt: Technical knowledge combining an engineering drawing, machine image, specification table, and graph
image.caption: Technical knowledge includes text, tables, drawings, equipment images, and graphs.

sections.title: Embeddings
content: An embedding is a numerical representation of meaning. Text with similar meaning tends to be placed near other text in a high-dimensional vector space, even when it uses different words.
An embedding model such as text-embedding-3-large converts a chunk or question into a vector. The vector is stored in a search index so semantic similarity can be calculated later.

sections.title: Vector Search
content: Vector search compares the question vector with indexed chunk vectors and returns semantically similar content. It can find a relevant passage even when the question does not use the exact wording in the document.
Vector search is not magic understanding. Quality depends on parsing, chunk boundaries, embedding choice, filters, index configuration, and the language and domain represented in the source material.

sections.title: Keyword Search and BM25
content: Keyword search looks for exact words, phrases, identifiers, model numbers, error codes, and abbreviations. BM25 is a ranking algorithm that scores documents using term frequency and document rarity.
Keyword search is especially valuable when a user knows a precise code or part number. It can miss paraphrases, synonyms, and conceptually similar wording that vector search can find.

sections.title: Hybrid Search
content: Hybrid search combines keyword and vector search. The two result lists are merged or fused so exact identifiers and semantic matches can both contribute evidence.

Azure AI Search supports hybrid retrieval patterns, while application code can tune weights, candidate counts, filters, and fallback behavior for the domain. Hybrid search is often a stronger default than choosing only one retrieval method.

sections.title: Metadata Filtering
content: Metadata filtering narrows retrieval using structured conditions such as site, language, product family, effective date, document status, or permission group. Filtering reduces noise and limits the candidate set before generation.
Security filters must be applied before evidence is returned to the model. A prompt instruction that says 'do not reveal confidential content' is not a substitute for query-time authorization.

sections.title: Reranking
content: Reranking reorders retrieved candidates using a stronger relevance model after an inexpensive first search. It helps the system place the most useful passages at the top of the context.
Azure Semantic Ranker is one option. Reranking adds latency and cost, so it should be used where the quality improvement justifies the extra work, with timeouts and fallback behavior.

sections.title: Context Construction
content: Context construction selects and formats evidence for the LLM. It should preserve source titles, page references, section headings, version dates, and clear boundaries between passages.

The context budget should reserve room for the answer. Sending every retrieved chunk increases cost and can make the model less focused. Deduplication and diversity rules help avoid repeating the same passage.

sections.title: Grounded Prompting
content: A grounded prompt tells the model to answer from supplied evidence, distinguish facts from uncertainty, and say when the evidence is insufficient. It can also specify response format, citation behavior, and safe escalation instructions.
Prompt templates should be versioned and tested. They should not be treated as the security boundary; identity, authorization, and retrieval filters must already be enforced by the application.

sections.title: Citations
content: A citation connects a statement to the document, version, page, section, or visual source that supports it. Citations make answers easier to verify and help experts quickly inspect the original context.
The application should generate citations from retrieval metadata rather than asking the model to invent links. A citation can be shown beside a sentence or in a sources panel.

sections.title: Hallucination Control
content: Hallucination control is a layered practice: retrieve relevant evidence, filter unauthorized material, require citations, constrain the prompt, validate the answer, and provide an abstention response when evidence is weak.
Useful signals include citation coverage, unsupported-claim rate, retrieval recall, answer correctness, and the percentage of questions escalated to a human. No single setting guarantees factuality.

sections.title: Document Versioning
content: Every indexed document should carry a stable identity and a version or effective date. When a new revision arrives, the system should know whether it supersedes, supplements, or merely duplicates an earlier source.
Version-aware retrieval prevents an old procedure from outranking a current one. Retention and rollback policies should preserve auditability without keeping obsolete content in active results.

sections.title: Duplicate Detection
content: Duplicate detection prevents the same content from being indexed repeatedly. A file checksum catches identical bytes; normalized text hashes and similarity checks can catch renamed or lightly modified copies.
Duplicates inflate storage, retrieval results, citations, and cost. Detection should be idempotent and should preserve the authoritative source rather than silently deleting provenance.

sections.title: Incremental Ingestion
content: Incremental ingestion processes only new, changed, or deleted sources instead of rebuilding the entire knowledge base. Change detection can use file fingerprints, source timestamps, webhooks, or content-management events.

A production job records checkpoints and failure states, retries transient errors, and publishes index changes atomically where possible. This keeps updates affordable and reduces the window in which search reflects mixed versions.

sections.title: Access Control and Security
content: Authentication answers who the user is; authorization answers what that user may access. Microsoft Entra ID can provide identity, while roles and groups can be mapped to document permissions. Managed Identity avoids putting service credentials in code.

Authorization must happen before retrieval. Permission metadata is applied as a search filter, and private content is never placed into the model context for an unauthorized request. Key Vault protects secrets, network isolation limits exposure, and audit logs record access decisions.

image.alt: Authorized access control protecting private technical documents in an AI knowledge system
image.caption: Access checks should ensure users retrieve only content they are authorized to see.

callouts: Do not retrieve first and filter later. Unauthorized evidence should never reach the prompt, logs, cache, or answer pipeline.

sections.title: Prompt Injection Protection
content: Prompt injection is content that tries to manipulate the assistant, for example by instructing it to ignore system rules or reveal hidden data. Retrieved documents must be treated as untrusted data, not as commands.

Use clear system instructions, separate evidence from instructions, strip or flag suspicious content, restrict tools, validate outputs, and require authorization outside the model. Test attacks against both user questions and documents.

sections.title: Evaluation
content: Evaluation measures whether the system retrieves the right evidence and produces a useful, supported answer. Build a representative question set with expected sources, permissions, difficulty, languages, and failure cases.

Track retrieval precision and recall, answer correctness, groundedness, citation accuracy, latency, cost, refusal quality, and access-control correctness. Human review remains important for ambiguous technical questions.

sections.title: Production Deployment
content: A production architecture separates development, QA, and production environments. FastAPI can expose a Python service, Pydantic can validate request and response shapes, and Docker can package repeatable deployments.

Azure DevOps can automate tests and releases. Deploy asynchronous ingestion workers separately from the query API, add retries and timeouts, use health checks, and support rollback to a known application and index version.

sections.title: Scalability
content: Scale ingestion and query workloads independently. Queue-based workers can process document spikes, while the query service can scale for active demand. Azure AI Search capacity, backend instances, database connections, and model quotas all affect throughput.

Total registered users are not the same as monthly active users. Simultaneous users influence infrastructure sizing, while query volume drives variable model, embedding, reranking, and transaction costs. Load tests should model realistic peaks.

sections.title: Monitoring and Observability
content: Observability makes system behavior explainable. Record correlation IDs, retrieval latency, model latency, token counts, selected sources, citation coverage, filter decisions, errors, retries, and cost estimates without logging sensitive document text unnecessarily.

Application Insights and Azure Monitor can support dashboards and alerts. Monitor quality drift as documents, models, prompts, indexes, and user behavior change. A useful alert should identify whether the issue is ingestion, retrieval, generation, security, or infrastructure.

image.alt: Illustrative dashboard monitoring query volume, response time, retrieval success, topics, cost, and alerts
image.caption: Illustrative example of operational metrics that can be monitored in a production RAG system.

sections.title: Model and Index Versioning
content: Embedding models, chunking rules, prompts, rerankers, and index schemas all influence results. Store their versions with each index build so a result can be reproduced and a change can be compared.
Blue-green or side-by-side indexes allow a new version to be evaluated before traffic moves. Keep rollback possible when relevance, cost, latency, or access behavior regresses.

sections.title: Cost Model
content: Ingestion pipeline cost is mainly document parsing, OCR, image or graph understanding, embeddings, and initial indexing. It is usually an upfront cost followed by incremental cost when sources are added or updated.

The user-query pipeline has a fixed baseline such as Azure AI Search, backend hosting, database, monitoring, and storage. Variable usage includes LLM calls, query embeddings, reranking, transactions, and logging. Active users, simultaneous users, and query volume affect different parts of this model.

steps: Ingestion: parse + OCR + understand visuals + embed + index
Query: authorize + embed + search + rerank + generate + cite

callouts: A large registered user base does not automatically mean high query cost. Monthly active users and questions per user drive usage, while concurrency drives capacity planning.

sections.title: Pilot-to-Production Roadmap
content: Start with a narrow, high-value document set and a measurable question set. Prove that the system can retrieve the right evidence, enforce access rules, produce useful citations, and meet an acceptable latency and cost target.

Then add more document types, roles, languages, visual content, update automation, evaluation coverage, and operational controls. A pilot should be designed as a thin slice of the production architecture, not as a disconnected demo.

sections.title: Key Takeaways
content: Enterprise RAG is a searchable, access-aware knowledge system connected to an LLM. Its value comes from the complete pipeline, not from the model alone.
Reliable results require good parsing, meaningful chunks, metadata, hybrid retrieval, reranking, citations, security before retrieval, evaluation, monitoring, and versioned operations.
The practical path is to start narrowly, measure honestly, and expand only when evidence shows the system is useful, secure, and affordable.

A small unit of text processed by a language model.
A numerical representation of meaning used for semantic similarity search.
Search based on semantic similarity between numerical representations.
Reordering retrieved results using a stronger relevance model.

A property where repeating an operation produces the same intended result without duplicates.
Constraining an answer to evidence supplied by the retrieval system.

takeaways: RAG connects an LLM to current, approved evidence.
Search quality depends on parsing, chunking, metadata, embeddings, keyword retrieval, hybrid search, and reranking.
Security and authorization must happen before retrieval and context construction.
Production readiness requires asynchronous jobs, retries, idempotency, versioning, evaluation, monitoring, and rollback.
A focused pilot can prove value before the organization expands coverage and capacity.
